extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, and newsroom professionals interested in news selection and organizational routines
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and organizational principles that shape which occurrences are recognized, gathered, and placed as news in newspapers and television — including beats, territoriality, staff vs stringers, editorial negotiation, budgets, and daily conferences. Focus is on how newsroom structures and routines produce newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for salaried reporters over stringers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors prefer stories by salaried reporters to those by stringers; the news organization has a financial investment in salaried reporters and tends to avoid stringers except in dire need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual evidence: bureau chiefs assert availability of their reporters to 'write copy like this story.' Photography editors rarely accept stringers' photos and will print a staff member’s shot 'even if the wire-service’s picture was photographically superior.' Television stations avoid using superior network footage if a station crew covered the story, and chastise crews instead. Stringers are used when an unexpected event occurs at night and no crew was assigned. Implication: use of staff reporters and staff-produced material is institutionally favored; relying on stringers is an anti-pattern unless unavoidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization at legitimated institutions (beat/bureau emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The news net privileges occurrences at centralized, legitimated institutions (e.g., City Hall, the United Nations), meaning events generated there are more likely to be identified as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: beats/bureaus at City Hall, UN, police, mayor’s office concentrate reporter attention; coverage reinforces legitimacy of institutions hosting beats. Small fish or occurrences in unassigned locations (e.g., working-class social movement debates) may be neglected. Organizational investment and routine presence at institutions shape what is deemed newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter/editorial status influences selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The hierarchical status of reporters in the news net may determine whose information is identified and selected as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: editors favor work produced by higher-status staff and those who are part of the organization's beats; bureau chiefs, metropolitan editors, and salaried reporters have institutional weight. This produces unequal consideration of material depending on reporter status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic territoriality (division of responsibility by place)
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations divide the world into areas of territorial responsibility; geographic territoriality is fundamental to dispersing reporters in space and to assumptions about readers’ interests in specific localities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalization: territorial desks (metropolitan, national, foreign) and local bureaus (boroughs, neighboring states) replicate the paper’s notion of its news mission and what readers want. Territorial responsibility often overrides other claims when multiple desks contest a story (proximity frequently decides assignment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational specialization (beats and topical departments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating beats and specialized topical departments (e.g., finance, sports, family/style, culture, education) organizes reporter responsibilities around organizations/topics and centralized information sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topical specialists may have separate offices, budgets, display control, and are expected to fill a set number of columns/pages. They can select pictures and layout for their pages. However, their work is still embedded in the broader newsroom bureaucracy and may be subordinate to territorial desks in daily operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of territoriality over topical specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Territorial desks typically take precedence over topical specialists in day-to-day claims to stories; physical proximity often determines who covers an event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: City Hall bureau claims nearby events even if topical editors believe the story belongs to them; reporters developing beats within a territorial bureau must operate within that territory (e.g., Hyde extending City Hall territory to nearby municipal offices). Conflicts are resolved case-by-case, with territorial proximity a decisive factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiated newsworthiness through editorial competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworthiness is constituted through negotiation and competition among reporters and editors; editors jockey to get their reporters’ stories placed and by-lines seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: editors and reporters engage in bargaining within the newsroom bureaucracy; the managing/executive editor coordinates competing claims. Daily routines (assignments, negotiations, jockeying for desks and by-lines) influence what is judged important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing/executive editor coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: The managing or executive editor coordinates territorial and topical editors, revises plans as the day progresses, and heads negotiations about which items are 'truly important news.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools available: wire-service budgets, desk budgets, knowledge of reporter assignments and unfolding events. The managing editor's role mitigates conflicts between desks by overseeing and reallocating resources and placements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of budgets and 'slugs' to plan resource allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire services and desks transmit daily budgets (a summary of how their reporters are being used) specifying a story's 'slug' and expected length; budgets propose how reporters and space/time will be spent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices: budgets list expected takes/feet of film; slugs identify a story’s essence and are attached to all related copy. Editors read and revise budgets to assess importance and potential page-one suitability. Budgets structure planning and allocation of scarce reporter/time resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily editorial conference and mutual determination of headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily editorial conferences (including executive/managing editor and territorial/topical editors) collectively code the merit of occurrences and decide front-page (or lead) placement through mutual assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process: each editor brings a list of reporter stories; editors ask 'What have you got?' and discuss significance. The group collectively sets boundaries of what can be considered important news at a moment; mutual agreements and compromises create the day's news hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance of interpersonal equilibrium to regulate offerings
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors maintain a careful equilibrium to prevent heated disputes; social norms and fear of being mocked for poor news judgment constrain what editors propose for front-page coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: topical editors rarely offer page-one stories (e.g., once a month) but succeed when they do because they know boundaries. Avoiding overt challenges preserves working relations and the daily accomplishment of news production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for flexibility in delineations of responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigid delineations of responsibility are avoided because news events are unpredictable; flexible negotiations are organizationally necessary to handle overlapping claims and unanticipated situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Times' rule that any reporter sent outside the U.S. reports to the international desk cannot fully specify in-trip responsibilities; traveling reporters often file for multiple desks. Flexibility allows the organization to act on unanticipated events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions about readers' interests (three assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally designed assumptions underlying the news net: (1) readers are interested in occurrences at specific localities, (2) they are concerned with activities of specific organizations, (3) they are interested in specific topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three assumptions justify geographic dispersion of reporters, focus on organizations, and highlighting of topics. They undergird territorial, organizational, and topical methods of reporter allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical departments' operational autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical departments have operational autonomy in some respects — fixed page/column expectations, control over display and picture selection, and separate offices shielding them from city-room observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: topical specialists are partially insulated from territorial monitoring (e.g., separate offices), can determine layout and picture selection for their departments, and are told how much space they must fill; yet they remain subordinate in certain conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance among desks as a measurable norm (Sigal's index)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal of balance among international, national, and metropolitan desks on page one exists; Sigal operationalized balance as variance from the ideal distribution and measured 'balance variation' to assess how pages conform to negotiated norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: compute ideal distribution for the day's number of stories (e.g., 12 stories -> 4-4-4) and sum absolute differences to actual distribution; days with large deviations or zero stories from a desk are 'imbalanced.' Data show Times and Post front pages are substantially balanced most days, reflecting ongoing editorial negotiation. This offers a quantitative rubric for assessing distributional equity of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureaucratic composition shapes topical prevalence
rubrics_metrics.description: The newsroom's bureaucratic composition (e.g., number of reporters on national vs international desks) shapes the relative frequency of story types — more national reporters yields more national stories over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: both Times and Post had more national than international reporters; wire-service budgets and resource availability produce a slight overrepresentation of national stories. Thus staff composition and budgetary allocations create structural biases in coverage.
